person.name: Edsger_W._Dijkstra
person.summary: Edsger W. Dijkstra was a Dutch computer scientist who developed foundational algorithms and methods for programming. He introduced Dijkstra's algorithm, semaphores, and major ideas in structured programming. He taught and conducted research in the Netherlands and the United States.

conclusion: Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm, semaphore work, and structured-programming ideas remain central reference points in computing. The ACM renamed its annual distributed-computing influential-paper award the Dijkstra Prize after his death.

events.title: Birth in Rotterdam
events.description: Edsger Wybe Dijkstra was born in Rotterdam, Netherlands, to Douwe Wybe Dijkstra and Brechtje Cornelia Kluijver. His father taught chemistry at a secondary school and later became its superintendent. His mother was a mathematician who never held a formal job.

events.title: Starts at the Mathematical Centre
events.description: In March 1952, Edsger W. Dijkstra began work at the Mathematical Centre, an Amsterdam research institute for mathematics and computing. Professor Johannes Haantjes introduced him to Adriaan van Wijngaarden, who offered him the post. Dijkstra was still completing theoretical-physics studies at Leiden.

events.title: Solves Shortest Path Problem
events.description: In 1956, Edsger W. Dijkstra formulated and solved the [[shortest-path problem|shortest-path problem]] while preparing a demonstration for [[ARMAC]], an early computer at Amsterdam’s Mathematical Centre. Carel S. Scholten and Bram Jan Loopstra built ARMAC. They worked with Dijkstra on its software.

event_class.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
event_class.description: It repeatedly selects the unvisited vertex with the lowest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges.
event_class.impact: The algorithm became a standard method for finding shortest paths in weighted networks.

shortest-path problem.explanation: A shortest-path problem asks for the least-cost route between points in a network. Dijkstra developed a procedure that finds those routes efficiently when connection costs are nonnegative.

ARMAC.explanation: ARMAC was an early Dutch electronic computer built at Amsterdam’s Mathematical Centre. Its development brought hardware designers and programmers together on one of the Netherlands’ first computer projects.

events.background:
Amsterdam’s Mathematisch Centrum had created a Computing Department under Adriaan van Wijngaarden in 1947. Van Wijngaarden visited England and the United States to gather ideas for the Netherlands’ first computer. The center’s first machine, the electromechanical ARRA, was demonstrated in 1952. Scholten and Loopstra had begun that work as physics students in 1947. Their ARRA I did not succeed. Gerrit Blaauw also worked on its successor, ARRA II. Work on the transistor-based ARMAC began in 1954. Its use of transistors was a notable feature at a time when electronic computers were still new. The center’s staff combined mathematics, physics, machine construction, and programming in the same project.

The group used an exact division of labor while the machine was being built. They first wrote a programming manual that fixed the interface between hardware and software. Scholten and Loopstra then had to build the machine according to that agreement. The software could be written against the manual before the hardware existed. Dijkstra later credited this arrangement with teaching him the value of clear documentation. He also concluded that careful design could prevent much of the debugging that programmers otherwise faced.

Automatic computing had no dedicated journals available to publish results from this work. The result associated with the ARMAC demonstration therefore remained unpublished until 1959. By then, the Mathematical Centre was also turning toward programming languages. Dijkstra and Jaap Zonneveld completed a compiler for ALGOL 60 in August 1960. The compiler was produced more than a year before another group made one. Scholten left the center for Electrologica in 1958. He and Loopstra developed the Electrologica X1 there, and 40 X1 machines had been installed by 1964, chiefly at universities.

events.title: Marries Maria Debets
events.description: In 1957, Edsger W. Dijkstra married Maria C. Debets in the Netherlands. At the ceremony, he gave his profession as programmer. Dutch authorities did not yet recognize that designation.

events.title: Earns Doctorate in Amsterdam
events.description: In 1959, Edsger W. Dijkstra received his doctorate from the University of Amsterdam under Adriaan van Wijngaarden. His thesis, Communication with an Automatic Computer, described [[assembly language|assembly language]] for the [[Electrologica X1]], an early Dutch computer.

assembly language.explanation: Assembly language uses short symbolic commands that correspond closely to a computer’s machine instructions. It gave programmers a readable way to direct a specific machine.

Electrologica X1.explanation: The Electrologica X1 was an early computer designed and built in the Netherlands. It was used at the Mathematical Centre for programming research and early compiler work.

events.title: Completes ALGOL 60 Compiler
events.description: On August 24, 1960, Edsger W. Dijkstra and Jaap A. Zonneveld completed an ALGOL 60 compiler at Amsterdam’s Mathematical Centre. ALGOL 60 was a new programming language. They worked day and night and kept duplicate notes in separate places in case their records were lost.

images.caption: Electrologica X1 console with ALGOL-60 compiler tapes
images.creator: PeterFrankfurt at German Wikipedia (Original text: de:Benutzer:PeterFrankfurt)

event_class.title: ALGOL 60 compiler
event_class.description: The compiler translates ALGOL 60 programs into instructions for the Electrologica X1 computer.
event_class.impact: It was the first completed compiler for the new ALGOL 60 programming language.

events.title: Moves to Eindhoven
events.description: In 1962, Dijkstra moved from Amsterdam to Eindhoven. He became a professor in the Mathematics Department at the Technische Hogeschool Eindhoven, the city’s technical university. He tried to build a group of computer scientists within the department.

events.title: Introduces Semaphores
events.description: In 1965, Dijkstra developed the [[semaphore|semaphore]] construct in Eindhoven. A semaphore is a programming tool that coordinates access to a shared resource. He was working on ways for several computer processes to run without interfering with one another.

event_class.title: Semaphores
event_class.description: Semaphore operations control access to shared resources by allowing processes to wait and signal one another.
event_class.impact: Semaphores became a basic tool for synchronization in operating systems and concurrent programs.

semaphore.explanation: Dijkstra introduced semaphores as operations that let one process wait for another or signal that a shared resource is available. They became a basic mechanism for coordinating concurrent tasks.

events.background:
The Technische Hogeschool Eindhoven housed computing within its Mathematics Department in the mid-1960s. It had no separate computer science department. The department’s culture did not particularly suit Dijkstra. He tried to gather computer scientists who could work together on problems. That arrangement was unusual within the department. The practical problem of coordinating work inside a machine belonged to a period when the academic identity of computer science itself was still unsettled.

His earlier work at Amsterdam’s Mathematisch Centrum had supplied a demanding model for such work. Dijkstra had worked with Bram Jan Loopstra and Carel S. Scholten while they built a computer. The three first wrote a programming manual that fixed the boundary between hardware and software. The hardware designers then had to keep their side of that agreement. Dijkstra wrote the software before the machine existed. He later said the experience taught him the value of clear documentation. He also concluded that careful design could prevent much of the debugging that programmers usually face afterward.

After moving to Eindhoven, he began circulating his own numbered manuscripts among colleagues. These papers came to be called EWDs from his initials. A long writer’s block followed the move, then a new EWD was photocopied and passed from recipient to recipient. The reports covered computer science and mathematics. They also included letters, speeches, and accounts of trips. The series eventually ran to more than 1,300 documents. In the late 1960s, work in the same Eindhoven setting produced the layered THE operating system. Its design used software-based paged virtual memory, and later operating-system designs drew on it.

events.title: Builds the THE System
events.description: In the late 1960s, Edsger W. Dijkstra built the THE multiprogramming system in Eindhoven. THE was a layered operating system that separated functions into levels. Its design used software-based paged virtual memory to manage the computer’s memory.

event_class.title: THE multiprogramming system
event_class.description: The layered operating system separates system functions and manages memory with software-based paged virtual memory.
event_class.impact: Its layered design and memory techniques influenced later operating system designs.

events.title: Challenges the Goto Statement
events.description: In March 1968, Edsger W. Dijkstra wrote Go To Statement Considered Harmful, a letter to the editor about [[goto statement|goto statements]] in computer programs. Communications of the ACM published the letter. Dijkstra argued that unrestricted jumps made programs harder to understand and verify.

goto statement.explanation: A goto statement transfers a program’s control to a labeled instruction elsewhere in the code. Such jumps were common in early programming languages.

event_class.title: Go To Statement Considered Harmful
event_class.impact: The article became a central statement in debates over structured programming and program correctness.

events.title: Receives Turing Award
events.description: In 1972, the [[Association for Computing Machinery|Association for Computing Machinery]] gave Edsger W. Dijkstra the [[Turing Award]]. The award recognized his fundamental contributions to programming languages and [[structured programming|structured programming]].

structured programming.explanation: Structured programming favors clear control patterns that make a program’s flow easier to follow and reason about. Dijkstra’s work made it central to debates about reliable software.

Association for Computing Machinery.explanation: The Association for Computing Machinery, usually called ACM, is a major international professional organization for computing.

Turing Award.explanation: The Turing Award is ACM’s leading annual award in computer science. It honors contributions of lasting importance to the field.

events.title: Joins Burroughs Research
events.description: In August 1973, Edsger W. Dijkstra joined [[Burroughs Corporation]], a computer manufacturer, as its sole research fellow. He worked mainly from his study in Nuenen. He visited the company’s United States research centers several times each year.

Burroughs Corporation.explanation: Burroughs Corporation was an American company that made business machines and computers. Its research-fellow arrangement allowed Dijkstra to continue working from the Netherlands.

events.background:
The Mathematics Department at the Technische Hogeschool Eindhoven had no separate computer science department. Its culture did not particularly suit Dijkstra. He had tried to assemble a group of computer scientists around shared problems within that setting. His new arrangement reduced his university appointment to one day a week. Tuesday became the day of the Tuesday Afternoon Club, a seminar that drew colleagues to discuss scientific articles.

The club treated an article as an object that could be examined line by line. Participants discussed its notation, organization, presentation, language, and content. This practice fitted Dijkstra's insistence on careful construction in technical writing. He composed most work alone. He handled his own correspondence. He also avoided using computers to write, working first with a typewriter and later with a Montblanc Meisterstück fountain pen.

His research output during these years filled the EWD series. Each manuscript carried his initials and a consecutive number. Most were technical reports circulated privately among a select group of colleagues. Recipients photocopied their copies and passed them to other scientists, creating an informal international distribution network. The subjects ranged across mathematics and computer science. Some papers also recorded trips, letters, and speeches. Almost all EWDs after 1972 were handwritten. They were usually no longer than 15 pages.

The series ultimately reached 1,318 documents. The last was dated April 14, 2002. The University of Texas maintains an archive where the EWDs have been scanned, with growing numbers transcribed for searching. The Tuesday Afternoon Club later acquired an Austin branch after Dijkstra accepted a University of Texas position in 1984.

events.title: Publishes A Discipline of Programming
events.description: In 1976, Dijkstra published A Discipline of Programming. The book treated program construction as a process of mathematical reasoning. It set out methods for proving that a program meets its intended requirements.

event_class.title: A Discipline of Programming
event_class.impact: The book became a major text for formal reasoning about program correctness.

events.title: Moves to the Austin Chair
events.description: In 1984, Edsger W. Dijkstra moved from Nuenen to Austin, Texas. He took the Schlumberger Centennial Chair in the Computer Science Department at the University of Texas at Austin. He taught and conducted research there until his retirement.

images.caption: Main Building, University of Texas at Austin
images.creator: Daderot

events.title: Retires to Nuenen
events.description: In November 1999, Edsger W. Dijkstra retired from the University of Texas at Austin. He and his wife, Maria C. Debets, returned to their home in Nuenen, Netherlands.

events.title: Dies in Nuenen
events.description: In Nuenen, Dijkstra learned that cancer left him only months to live. He died there on August 6, 2002, after a long struggle with the illness.
events.background:
At the University of Texas at Austin, the computer science department had created the Schlumberger Centennial Chair for him in 1984. His teaching there followed rules of his own. He photographed every student at the beginning of a semester so he could learn each name. His courses focused on presenting mathematical proofs. He wrote proofs in chalk and examined students orally for several hours at a time. The department held a symposium for his seventieth birthday in May 2000 to recognize more than four decades of work in computing.

His household in Nuenen remained deliberately spare. The small house had no television, video player, or mobile telephone. He played piano and listened closely to classical music. Mozart was his favorite composer. He used a Montblanc Meisterstück fountain pen for his work. He composed arguments in his head before committing them to paper. He had developed that habit as a physics student while walking Leiden’s streets.

His handwritten manuscripts, numbered EWD after his initials, continued this method of work. Each was copied and circulated privately among colleagues, who in turn copied and passed it onward. The series covered computer science, mathematics, letters, speeches, and travel reports. It eventually reached 1,318 documents. The final EWD bears the date April 14, 2002.

Shortly before the end of his life, the Association for Computing Machinery gave him its PODC Influential-Paper Award for work on self-stabilization, a way for a distributed computer system to recover from faults. His family accepted a 2002 C&C Foundation of Japan award after his death. In 2003, the annual distributed-computing paper award was renamed the Edsger W. Dijkstra Prize. The University of Texas began its Dijkstra Memorial Lecture in 2010, with Tony Hoare as the first speaker.
